Vedic texts already mention drums and rhythm, and small drums appear in second-century BC carvings at the Bhaja caves and in fifth-century paintings at Ajanta. In the Middle Ages drum names such as pushkara appear in temple carvings and texts, and the name 'tabla' appears later, possibly from an Arabic word for drum. Clear images exist after about 1745, and the drum's shape was still changing into the early nineteenth century. After the eighteenth century it became the main percussion of Hindustani classical music, and it spread with devotional singing, Sufi music and Kathak dance across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka.

Its range runs from the middle-high to the low register, producing sounds from a crisp stroke to a muffled boom. The bayan (bass drum) is heavier and darker, in clear contrast with the bright tone of the dayan (treble drum). By changing the striking point, the force and the finger technique the player produces many different timbres on the same head. Its resonance is distinctive, relying on the drumhead and the cavity to produce rich overtones. Beside the crisp dryness of a Western drum kit the tabla has a warmer and more complex Eastern tone, with great expressive power and an unmistakable identity.

The bayan is the bass drum of the tabla pair, a membranophone with the Hornbostel–Sachs number 211.11. The body is traditionally clay and is now mostly cast in copper, tin or other metals in a cup shape, about 20 cm across, and its pitch is usually an octave or a fifth below the dayan. A black tuning paste of iron filings, flour and glue is pasted at the centre of the head, which gives the head overtones close to whole-number ratios; the head is fixed with leather straps threaded through holes, with small wooden pegs wedged in, and the rim can be struck with a small hammer to adjust the tension. The player strikes the centre and the edge of the head with the palm or fingers, and the heel of the left palm can press the head and slide forward to change the pitch. It is commonly used to accompany North Indian classical music and South Asian traditional music, and for rhythmic playing.
演奏時以右手擊高音鼓達顏（Dayan），左手擊低音鼓巴顏（Bayan）。發聲主要: Play by striking the treble drum, the dayan, with the right hand and the bass drum, the bayan, with the left. The sound comes mainly from the palm and fingers striking the centre and the edge of the head, and different points and ways of pressing give different pitches; the heel of the left palm, for instance, can press the head and slide forward to change the tension of the drumhead and so the pitch. Beginners can first practise each hand's striking point separately, then build rhythm patterns (theka) from drum syllables (bol), and vary the rhythm over the cyclical avartan.
